source.title: Enhancing generalization in high energy physics using white-box adversarial attacks
source.authors: F. Rothen; S. Klein; M. Leigh; T. Golling

record.file_problem: The full article text is present. No material cutoff or garbling affects the extracted results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial training methods that reduce measured loss sharpness improve cross-simulator generalization, using a dense network and cross-evaluation between Pythia and Herwig.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own cross-evaluation and sharpness results. Cited results from prior work are excluded. It does not test the listed same-distribution generalization versions; its cross-simulator evaluation is out-of-distribution.
record.test_reason: The study uses the broader flat-minima hypothesis to design adversarial training and reports its performance on simulator transfer. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, reduced Hessian eigenvalues and unscaled gradient-ascent loss changes in a dense jet classifier do not measure V7's magnitude-aware weight perturbations or their ranking of training–test gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: simulator transfer exposes performance losses, adversarial training improves transfer and reduces sharpness in its targeted space, and the authors identify PGD as most effective overall. Qualify that ranking: SSAMD has the largest reported Pythia-to-Herwig gains, whereas PGD leads Herwig-to-Pythia. The authors also acknowledge increased computational cost and leave transfer to real data unverified.
record.recipe_differences: Uses four adversarial training methods on a dense HEP classifier and evaluates cross-simulator performance; it does not use the original studies' random-label, width-sweep, image-architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness-gap, or memorized-example protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: The direction of cross-evaluation changes relative performance: feature-space attacks generalize better Herwig→Pythia, while weight-space attacks show the opposite trend. Feature-space attacks reduce feature-space sharpness; weight-space methods reduce weight-space sharpness. FGSM and PGD have different cross-evaluation gains; PGD is reported as overall most effective.

fits_no_version.finding: All four adversarial methods improve the reported simulator-transfer scores, with gains depending on method and transfer direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this dense jet classifier under the tested training budget, adversarial training recovers part of the performance deficit between cross-simulator evaluation and a default model trained on the destination simulator.

fits_no_version.finding: Sharpness changes depend on the perturbation space: feature attacks chiefly flatten feature space, while SAM methods flatten weight space; flattening in one space need not flatten the other.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this dense jet classifier, adversarial training changes reduced Hessian curvature differently in feature space and the final classification layer. These measurements do not establish a magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.

record.problems: The paper evaluates generalization across only two Monte Carlo simulators, not real-world data. Sharpness is approximated using reduced feature and weight subspaces; the paper notes computational limits. Results are averages and standard deviations over five random seeds. Cross-simulator evaluation is out-of-distribution and does not establish the same-distribution training-test gap in the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: Table X repeats the Hessian comparisons for additional train/evaluation scenarios; omitted to keep within the 60-row limit and avoid duplicating the 20 Table IV measurements. Gradient-ascent sharpness curves in Figures 3 and 7 are figure-only and not separately extracted because the paper describes the qualitative pattern and reports Hessian values in tables. Raw-score Table IX and same-simulator performance curves in Figures 4–5 are not extracted because the main cross-simulator performance rows are reported in Table V and the paper says same-simulator differences are slight.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy under matched architectures and recipes.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and their dependence on tuning, weight decay, or switching. All methods here use AdamW.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes. Batch size is fixed at 128, with a 24-hour training limit.
Dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout with weight decay under augmentation.

Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Neither Hessian tables nor same-simulator performance curves supply these comparisons.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and resulting test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed against the supplied versions; cannot_determine does not deny the reported transfer gains or curvature changes. Equation (14) normalizes improvement by the default transfer deficit. Table IV values are faithfully extracted, although Table X contains minor discrepancies for some repeated entries. No omitted result bears on V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and same-distribution held-out performance.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and same-distribution test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures on image datasets.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance under the stated tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its relation to the same-distribution training-test gap; the paper measures reduced Hessian eigenvalues and cross-simulator performance instead.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
